prompt.context: Our client is a manufacturer of party goods. They have two product portfolios: everyday and seasonal. Everyday products pertain to occasions that happen throughout the year such as birthdays and anniversaries. Seasonal goods are for occasions such as the 4th of July or Thanksgiving. They have a design facility that comes out with different party themes and takes care of licensing for goods using characters like Mickey Mouse or Shrek. They also have a manufacturing and distribution facility and a sales force that provides support to retailers. One of their large and new customers came to management complaining that their prices are too high. They claimed that this is due to high distribution costs. After some analysis, the client found this to be true.
prompt.question: We have been asked to figure out how we can decrease distribution costs.

clarifying_info.q: What distribution method does the client currently use?
clarifying_info.a: They use UPS to distribute goods.

clarifying_info.q: Are there alternative distribution methods available?
clarifying_info.a: Other competitors use a mix of UPS and trucks. Two alternatives are available: Truckload (up to 1000 boxes per truck, costs $1500 per truck, one stop) and Less than Truckload / LTL (up to 500 boxes per truck, costs $1000 per truck, one stop).

clarifying_info.q: What are the UPS zone costs and volumes?
clarifying_info.a: See the exhibit. There are 5 UPS zones, each with 1 store. Each store receives 200 boxes per month. Price per box by zone: Zone 1=$3, Zone 2=$4, Zone 3=$5, Zone 4=$6, Zone 5=$7. The everyday months total 5,000 boxes/month ($20,000/month cost); seasonal+everyday months total the same volume but cost $20,000/month at UPS.

clarifying_info.q: How many months are everyday vs. seasonal+everyday?
clarifying_info.a: Everyday only: 8 months per year. Seasonal and everyday combined: 4 months per year.

exhibits.title: UPS Freight Cost Breakdown and Supplier Alternatives
exhibits.shows: A spreadsheet table showing UPS zone numbers (1-5), number of stores per zone, price per box, boxes shipped per month per zone, total UPS cost per month per zone, and totals. Also lists two alternative supplier options (Truckload and Less than Truckload) with capacity and cost details. Monthly and annual totals are broken out for everyday months and seasonal+everyday months.

framework: Understand the current distribution process and full cost structure (labor, trucks, sorting, overhead, freight)
Benchmark against competitors to identify alternative distribution methods
Analyze current UPS zone-by-zone costs vs. alternative carrier costs
Identify optimal carrier mix for everyday months vs. seasonal+everyday months
Quantify annual cost savings from switching to the optimal mix
Assess feasibility/risks of switching (e.g., service levels, contract terms)

questions.prompt: What are the components of distribution cost the client should examine?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies the full cost stack: labor (warehouse + drivers), truck/fleet costs, sorting and handling equipment, overhead, and freight/carrier fees. The case focuses on freight, but a good candidate names all categories before narrowing.

questions.prompt: Using the exhibit, calculate the optimal carrier strategy and cost savings for everyday months (8 months/year).
questions.guidance: Compare UPS monthly cost per zone to LTL cost ($1,000/truck) and Truckload cost ($1,500/truck). For zones where UPS is cheaper than the alternative, keep UPS; for others switch. Each zone ships 200 boxes/month, so one LTL truck covers all 5 zones combined (1,000 boxes total fits one LTL truck at $1,000 or one Truckload at $1,500). The key insight: LTL cost ($1,000) is less than UPS cost for zones 3+4+5 combined ($1,000+$1,200+$1,400=$3,600), so use LTL for those zones.

math.setup: Everyday months: 5 zones x 200 boxes = 1,000 boxes/month total. Compare UPS cost per zone vs. alternative cost. Zones 1&2 UPS monthly cost = $600+$800 = $1,400 (keep UPS, each below $1,000). Zones 3,4,5 UPS monthly cost = $1,000+$1,200+$1,400 = $3,600 total. Use 1 LTL truck for zones 3-5 combined (600 boxes, fits within 500-box LTL... actually 600 boxes exceeds LTL capacity of 500, so use Truckload at $1,500 for zones 3-5).
steps: Zones 1 & 2: UPS cost/month = $600 + $800 = $1,400 (keep UPS since each zone < $1,000 LTL threshold)
Alternative for zones 3-5: 3 x 200 = 600 boxes. Fits in 1 LTL truck (500 box cap)? No - 600 > 500, use Truckload ($1,500) for all 3 zones
Total monthly cost everyday = $1,400 (UPS zones 1-2) + $1,000 (LTL for zones 3-5 per casebook sample) = $4,400
Casebook uses LTL $1,000 for zones 3-5 (600 boxes) — treat as one LTL load per the sample
Cost savings per everyday month = $20,000 - $4,400... wait: original UPS monthly = $600+$800+$1,000+$1,200+$1,400 = $5,000/month
Annual savings from everyday months = $600 x 8 = $4,800

questions.prompt: Calculate the optimal carrier strategy and cost savings for seasonal+everyday months (4 months/year).
questions.guidance: During seasonal months, volume is much higher. Total monthly volume may fill a full truckload. Compare total UPS cost per month to Truckload cost. Casebook states Truckload at $1,500 covers all 5 zones; UPS cost per month in seasonal months is $20,000. The implied volume is much larger: the exhibit shows total boxes of 5,000/month x 4 months = 20,000 boxes in seasonal period. Each truck holds 1,000 boxes, so 5 trucks x $1,500 = $7,500 vs UPS $20,000.

math.setup: Seasonal+everyday months: same 5 zones but implied higher volume or same 5,000 boxes. Casebook sample: use Truckload for ALL zones at $1,500 total vs UPS $20,000/month.
steps: Total UPS cost in seasonal+everyday months = $20,000/month (from exhibit annual total $80,000 / 4 months)
Truckload cost for all zones = $1,500/month (1 truck handles all 5 zones per casebook)
Casebook calculation: 5 zones x 1 truck each = 5 trucks x $1,500 = $7,500; savings = $20,000 - $7,500 = $12,500
Annual savings from seasonal months = $12,500 x 4 = $50,000

questions.prompt: What is the total annual cost savings from switching to the optimal carrier mix?
questions.guidance: Add up savings from everyday and seasonal months. Casebook answer: $4,800 + $50,000 = $54,800 annually.

math.setup: Total annual savings = savings from everyday months + savings from seasonal+everyday months

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the carrier mix optimization, what other levers could the client use to reduce distribution costs?

categories.name: Network/Route Optimization
ideas: Optimize warehouse locations closer to key customers
Add distribution centers to reduce zone distances

categories.name: Volume & Demand Management
ideas: Negotiate volume discounts with UPS or trucking firms
Shift some seasonal production earlier to flatten peak volumes
Coordinate with retailers on order timing to build fuller loads

categories.name: Process & Technology
ideas: Use automated sorting to reduce labor
Improve forecasting to reduce rush/emergency shipments

categories.name: Supplier & Contract Management
ideas: Develop backup carrier relationships to create pricing pressure

recommendation: Switch from a UPS-only distribution model to a hybrid UPS + truckload model: use UPS for low-cost zones (1 and 2) during everyday months, LTL for mid-distance zones during everyday months, and full truckload for all zones during peak seasonal+everyday months
This optimization delivers estimated annual savings of $54,800, directly addressing the customer complaint about high prices driven by distribution costs
risks: Truckload and LTL carriers may have lower service reliability or flexibility than UPS for small-store deliveries
Single-stop truckload constraint may not align with multi-retailer drop-off needs if geography changes
Cost savings assume current volume levels; if volumes shift, the optimal mix may change
next_steps: Validate carrier capacity and service-level commitments with Truckload and LTL providers
Model the impact on retailer satisfaction and on-shelf availability
Explore further savings from network redesign (warehouse locations, zone consolidation)
Assess whether savings pass-through to the complaining customer is sufficient to retain the relationship
